1.title: Networking and Service Mesh
1.text: Welcome to Module 6: Networking and Service Mesh. This module is in the Container Orchestration domain, and it covers the topic called Networking. By the end you will be able to do four things. Explain the network model and the role of C N I plugins. Choose a Service type and trace how D N S and kube proxy deliver traffic. Route outside traffic with Ingress and Gateway A P I. And restrict traffic with a Network Policy, and recognize a service mesh.

1.title: Case Check-In: Harbor Books Connects Its Parts
1.text: At Harbor Books, the storefront, catalog, orders and postgres Pods must find each other, even as Pods are replaced. Each part needs a stable address, and visitors need a route from the internet to the storefront. Only orders may call postgres, and every other Pod must be kept out. In this module you build the network around the shop.

1.title: The Kubernetes Network Model
1.text: The Kubernetes network model is simple. Every Pod gets its own unique I P address, valid across the whole cluster. Containers in one Pod share a network namespace, and reach each other on localhost. Any Pod can reach any other Pod directly, with no proxy and no N A T, network address translation, even on another node. And agents on a node, such as the kube let, can reach all Pods on that node. The diagram also shows who hands out addresses. The network plugin assigns Pod I Ps, the kube A P I server assigns Service I Ps, and the kube let or the cloud controller manager assigns Node I Ps. Exam tip: Pod I Ps come from the network plugin, and Service I Ps from the A P I server.

1.title: CNI and Network Plugins
1.text: This slide is tagged beyond the curriculum. A C N I plugin, for Container Network Interface, implements the network model. It gives Pods their addresses and connects them. A cluster needs a C N I plugin, and the choice changes features such as Network Policy support. Cilium has a dataplane based on e B P F, for networking, observability and security, and it enforces network policy up to the application layer. Calico is a C N I network plugin with network policy support. And Flannel is a simple layer three fabric, where the flanneld agent gives each host a subnet. Exam tip: a C N I plugin builds the Pod network, and policy enforcement depends on the plugin.

1.title: Services: A Stable Address for Pods
1.text: Pods are replaced often, and each replacement has a new I P. So other parts cannot rely on a Pod address. A Service gives a set of Pods one stable name and virtual I P. A label selector chooses which Pods belong to the Service. In the diagram, the storefront calls the catalog Service, and Kubernetes load balances the traffic over the three catalog Pods that match. When Pods come and go, the Service address stays. Exam tip: a Service finds its Pods by labels, not by names.

1.title: Service Types
1.text: There are five kinds to know. Cluster I P is the default. It is a virtual I P inside the cluster, reachable only from within it. Node Port opens the same port on every node, from a default range of thirty thousand to thirty-two thousand, seven hundred and sixty-seven, on top of a Cluster I P. Load Balancer uses an external load balancer, which Kubernetes does not provide itself. A cloud provider usually does. External Name answers with a C name, an alias record, for an outside D N S name, with no proxying. And a headless Service sets cluster I P to None. It has no virtual I P, and D N S returns the Pod I Ps. Exam tip: Cluster I P is the default, and Node Port and Load Balancer expose a Service outside.

1.title: A Service Manifest
1.text: Here is a Service for the catalog Pods. The selector picks the Pods by their labels, here app equals catalog. Port is the port that clients call, and target port is the port in the container, here eighty and eighty-eighty. If you leave out target port, it is the same as port. And the type defaults to Cluster I P, which the snippet states for clarity. Exam tip: port is what clients call, and target port is where the container listens.

1.title: EndpointSlices and kube-proxy
1.text: How does a Service find its Pods? For a Service with a selector, Kubernetes creates Endpoint Slices automatically. They list the addresses of the matching Pods. A slice holds at most one hundred endpoints by default, so a big Service has several slices. The older Endpoints A P I is deprecated. Then kube proxy, which runs on each node, sets up the rules that send Service traffic to those addresses. On Linux it works in i p tables, i p v s or n f tables mode. A headless Service is not handled by kube proxy. Exam tip: the Service is the name, the Endpoint Slice is the list, and kube proxy is the plumbing.

1.title: DNS, CoreDNS and Service Discovery
1.text: Pods find a Service in two ways, D N S and environment variables. The kube let adds variables ending in service host and service port to new Pods, named after the Service. So the Service must exist before the Pod. D N S has no ordering problem. A Service named orders in the namespace shop is orders dot shop dot svc dot cluster dot local. A Pod can use the short name for a Service in its own namespace, and for another namespace it adds the namespace, as in orders dot shop. Core D N S, a C N C F graduated project, is the cluster D N S add-on, and it answers these names. Exam tip: same namespace, short name. Other namespace, name dot namespace.

1.title: Ingress: HTTP Routes into the Cluster
1.text: An Ingress routes H T T P and H T T P S traffic from outside the cluster to Services, using rules on host and path. But an Ingress is only rules. An Ingress controller must be running to act on them. The ingress class name field says which controller handles an Ingress. In the diagram, visitors reach the controller, which sends the root path to the storefront Service and the orders path to the orders Service. The Ingress A P I is frozen. It stays and is stable, but it gets no new features. Exam tip: no Ingress controller, no routing.

1.title: Gateway API and the Ingress NGINX Retirement
1.text: This slide is tagged moving. Gateway A P I is the successor to Ingress. It is an add-on that is role-oriented, portable, expressive and extensible. Its stable kinds include Gateway Class, a set of gateways with common configuration. Gateway, the entry point that actually takes in traffic, for example a cloud load balancer. H T T P Route, which maps H T T P traffic from a Gateway to backends, often Services. And G R P C Route, the same for g R P C traffic. As of the thirtieth of October, twenty twenty-six, the Ingress Nginx controller was retired in March, twenty twenty-six. There are no more releases, bug fixes or security updates, but existing installations keep working. The advice is to move to Gateway A P I or another Ingress controller. Exam tip: Gateway A P I replaces Ingress for new designs.

1.title: LoadBalancer Without a Cloud: MetalLB
1.text: This slide is tagged beyond the curriculum. A Service of type Load Balancer needs an external load balancer, and Kubernetes does not provide one itself. On a cloud provider, the provider's integration creates it. On your own hardware, which is called bare metal, an add-on does the job. Metal L B fills that gap for bare-metal clusters, with an implementation built on standard routing protocols. Exam tip: Load Balancer needs something to make the load balancer, a cloud, or Metal L B on bare metal.

2.title: NetworkPolicy: Rules for Pod Traffic
2.text: By default, Pods are non-isolated, and all inbound and outbound traffic is allowed. A Network Policy that selects a Pod makes it isolated for that direction, and then only allowed traffic gets through. Policies are additive. They never conflict, and the allowed traffic is the union of their rules. Rules select peers with pod Selector, namespace Selector or I P Block. The network plugin enforces policies, and without support a policy has no effect. The snippet lets only orders Pods reach postgres. Exam tip: open by default, and once a policy selects a Pod, only what policies allow gets in.

2.title: Service Mesh: Sidecar and Sidecarless
2.text: This slide is tagged archived topic. A service mesh manages traffic between services, and adds reliability, observability and security the same way for all of them, without code changes. In the sidecar design, a proxy beside each app container intercepts its traffic and enforces policy, at the cost of more resources. In the sidecarless design, the work moves out of the Pods, for example into the kernel with e B P F. Examples are Istio, with Envoy sidecars and an ambient mode without them, and Linkerd. A common feature is mutual T L S. Exam tip: a mesh handles traffic between services, and Ingress and Gateway A P I handle traffic coming in.

2.title: What the Exam Asks: Networking
2.text: Six pairs to keep apart. Pod I P or Service I P: a Pod has its own I P from the network plugin, and a Service gives a stable virtual I P. Cluster I P, Node Port or Load Balancer: inside only, a port on every node, or an external load balancer. Service or Ingress: a Service exposes Pods, and an Ingress routes H T T P by host and path to Services. Ingress or Gateway A P I: Gateway A P I is the successor, and both need a controller or implementation. Kube proxy or Core D N S: kube proxy sets up forwarding rules, and Core D N S answers names. And Network Policy: open by default, additive, and it needs a plugin that enforces it. Exam tip: name the layer first.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: To recap. The network model gives one I P to every Pod, with direct traffic and no N A T, and a C N I plugin builds it. A Service is a stable name and virtual I P over a label-selected set of Pods, in the types Cluster I P, Node Port, Load Balancer, External Name and headless. Behind a Service, Endpoint Slices list the Pods, kube proxy programs the rules, and Core D N S answers the names. From outside, Ingress needs a controller, Gateway A P I is the successor, and Metal L B serves bare metal. A Network Policy is open by default, additive, and enforced by the plugin. And a service mesh adds security, reliability and observability. Now nine practice questions.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Which statement describes the Kubernetes network model? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Every Pod gets its own unique I P, valid across the cluster, and Pods communicate directly without proxies or N A T. Only the containers of one Pod share a network namespace.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. The Harbor Books storefront must call the catalog Pods, which are replaced often and get new I Ps each time. What gives the storefront a stable address to call? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. A Service gives the Pods that match its selector one stable name and virtual I P, however often individual Pods change. A Config Map would need manual updates, a Node Port points at one node, and restarting the storefront does not give it an address.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Which Service type uses an external load balancer, for example one from a cloud provider? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. The Load Balancer type exposes a Service through an external load balancer, which Kubernetes does not provide itself. A cloud provider usually does. Cluster I P stays inside the cluster, External Name only maps a name, and a headless Service has no virtual I P.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. A storefront Pod in the namespace shop must call the Service orders in the namespace backend. Which name does it use? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. The short name only works for a Service in the Pod's own namespace. For another namespace the name is the Service name followed by the namespace, here orders dot backend, or the full form orders dot backend dot svc dot cluster dot local.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Harbor Books created an Ingress with host and path rules for the storefront, but no traffic reaches the Pods. What is a likely cause? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. An Ingress is only a set of rules, and an Ingress controller must be running to act on them. The Ingress A P I is frozen but not removed, it can be created in any namespace, and rules can match both host and path.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Which statement about Gateway A P I and Ingress is correct? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Gateway A P I is the successor to Ingress and is role-oriented, with kinds such as Gateway Class, Gateway and H T T P Route. Routes usually point at Services, and the Ingress A P I is frozen but still available.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. A namespace has no Network Policy. Which traffic is allowed to and from its Pods? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Pods are non-isolated by default, so with no policy all inbound and outbound traffic is allowed. A Pod becomes isolated for a direction only when a policy selects it.

2.title: Practice Question 8
2.text: Question eight. Harbor Books applies a Network Policy that lets only the orders Pods reach postgres, yet other Pods still connect. Which cause is most likely? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. The network plugin does the enforcing, and a policy without a plugin that supports it has no effect. Policies apply to any selected Pods, need no matching policy on the callers, and are additive rather than overriding.

2.title: Practice Question 9
2.text: Question nine. What does a service mesh provide for the services of a cluster? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. A service mesh manages the traffic between services and adds reliability, observability and security uniformly, usually with proxies, without changes to application code. Storage, image builds and scheduling belong to other parts of the platform.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are the answers at a glance. Question one, C: one I P per Pod, and direct traffic with no N A T. Question two, A: a Service with a selector gives a stable address. Question three, D: Load Balancer uses an external load balancer. Question four, B: for a Service in another namespace, use name dot namespace. Question five, B: an Ingress needs a running controller. Question six, D: Gateway A P I is the successor to Ingress. Question seven, A: Pods are non-isolated by default. Question eight, C: the plugin must enforce Network Policy. Question nine, A: a mesh adds security, reliability and observability.
